767 παρασύρας Choerob. cod. V et Etym. M.: παρὰ συρὰν Choerob. codd. NC

767 Choerob. in Theod. p. 278, 27 [=267, 6 Hilgard] ἡ ἴκτινα αἰτιατικὴ... οὐκ ἔστιν ὡς ἀπὸ τῆς ἴκτιν εὐθείας,...ἀλλ᾿ ἔστιν ἴκτινος ἡ εὐθεῖα, ὡς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ· ‘ἴκτινος...κρέας.’ Etym. M. p. 470, 103 (p. 1345 Gaisf.)=Etym. Flor. ed. Miller p. 167, and Zonar. lex. p. 1100 ἴκτινος ἔκλαγξε (ἔκραξε cod. Haun. and Zonar.) παρασύρας κρέας.

παρασύρας expresses the swiftly swooping movement of the kite as he descends upon his food, and snatches it away without faltering. Neither L. and S.'s ‘filch,’ nor Campbell's ‘as it tears at the carrion’ is satisfactory. Ellendt's praetervolando trahere is better, but fails to give the exact force of παρασύρειν. The proper application of the word is to a river in full flood sweeping away every obstacle: see lexx. and the metaphorical use in [Longin.] de sublim. 32. 4 τῷ ῥοθίῳ τῆς φορᾶς ταυτὶ (sc. τὰ πάθη) πέφυκεν ἅπαντα τἄλλα παρασύρειν καὶ προωθεῖν. —Choerob.'s reading suggested παρασύρων to Blaydes, but the aor. is better. — For the accentuation of ἴκτινος (ἰκτῖνος) see Chandler, § 290, and for the general sense cf. Semonid. fr. 11 σπλάγχν’ ἀμφέποντες αὐτίκ’ ἰκτίνου δίκην.

lines.text: φυσᾷ γὰρ οὐ σμικροῖσιν αὐλίσκοις ἔτι,

fragments.context:
768

768 Cic. Att. 2. 16. 2 Gnaeus quidem noster iam plane quid cogitet nescio, ‘φυσᾷ γὰρ . . . ἄτερ.’ [Longinus] de subl. 3. 2 φλοιώδης γὰρ ἁνὴρ καὶ φυσῶν κατὰ τὸν Σοφοκλέα μικροῖς μὲν αὐλίσκοισι, φορβειᾶς δ’ ἄτερ.

Welcker assigned these lines to the Orithyia, and there has been a lively controversy whether Sophocles actually wrote a play with such a title. It must be observed in the first place that Longinus and Cicero do not agree, and that, if they are referring to the same passage, either Longinus is quoting inaccurately or his text is corrupt (οὐ σμικροῖς Toll, and so Wecklein). For the bearing of this on the interpretation of σμικροὶ αὐλίσκοι see below. Immisch (Rh. Mus. XLVIII 512) infers that Cicero's quotation is from a different original, and that it should be removed to the tragic adespota. But it is difficult to believe that two passages so nearly identical, and both familiar in their rhetorical application, were entirely independent of each other. Immisch has left out of account the possibility that Longinus adapted the quotation from Sophocles to suit his particular contention, that bombast is especially contemptible if coming from an inferior artist — a possibility which applies equally well, if we accept Immisch's interpretation of αὐλίσκοι and φορβειά. Marx (Wiener Stud. XX 191) for different reasons arrives at a conclusion similar to that of Immisch, that Aeschylus wrote the lines quoted by Cicero, and that Sophocles imitated them (cf. fr. 805). He is then obliged to assume that Longinus quoted the passage of Sophocles twice in a similar context, but with an entirely different purpose in either case. The assumption is improbable and gives too much weight to the precarious evidence of Iohannes Siceliota. That Sophocles compared a violent utterance to an inartistic performance by a flute-player appears to be certain. But what is there to show that he was speaking of Boreas? Or, even if so, that the quotation belonged to an Orithyia? The only direct evidence in favour of an affirmative answer is fr. 805, where see note. Some weight ought perhaps also to be attached to fr. 956. Since the allusion to Orithyia occurs not in a chorus but in an iambic narrative, it is natural to infer that it was relevant to the main action of the play in which it occurred. Buecheler in Rh. Mus. xxxix 274 agreed with Welcker, thinking that Sophocles imitated and criticized the Orithyia of Aeschylus in a play written under the same title. On the whole, I prefer to follow G. Wolff, who in Philol. XXVIII 343 argued that the existence of an Orithyia was not established, and referred fr. 956 to the Tympanistae.

φυσᾷ appears to be used here with metaphorical import, as our ‘blow’ is employed dialectically in the sense of ‘to blow one's own trumpet.’ See Headlam on Herond. 2. 32, and cf. Dem. 19. 314 τὰς γνάθους φυσῶν, describing the self-importance of Aeschines, Hyperid. fr. 91 K. (Athen. 591 F) οὐ σιωπήσῃ, μειράκιον, μεῖζον τῆς μητρὸς ἔχων τὸ φύσημα; addressed to Demeas, the son of an αὐλητρίς, who had been adopted by Demades. There was something ridiculous to the Athenians in the puffed-out cheeks of the flute-player (Plut. Alcib. 2), and this feeling contributed towards the aesthetic objection which made them speak contemptuously of the flute. Hence the epigram (Athen. 337 E): ἀνδρὶ μὲν αὐλητῆρι θεοὶ νόον οὐκ ἐνέφυσαν, | ἀλλ’ ἅμα τῷ φυσῆν χὠ νόος ἐκπέταται. This contempt was symbolized for them in the legend which represented Athena as throwing away the flute in disgust at the disfigurement which it caused (Melanippides fr. 2, 3, Telestes fr. 1, 3), and Marsyas as having subsequently picked it up; and was not the less cherished because flute-playing happened to be the favourite art of the despised Boeotians (Plut. l.c., Ar. Ach. 862 ff., Plat. rep. 399 E, Frazer on Pausan. 1. 24. 1). Here the diminutive αὐλίσκοι is significant; the plural (cf. αὐλοί) refers to the double flute: see Dict. Ant. II 840 (s.v. tibia), where also the contrivance of the φορβειά is explained. Its absence suggests that the player was not a skilled musician or properly equipped: see Ar. Vesp. 582 κἂν αὐλητής γε δίκην νικᾷ, ταύτης ἡμῖν ἐπίχειρα | ἐν φορβειᾷ τοῖσι δικασταῖς ἔξοδον ηὔλησ’ ἀπιοῦσιν. Cf. the account of its invention by Marsyas: Plut. cohib. ir. 6 p. 456 C φορβειᾷ τινι καὶ περιστομίοις τοῦ πνεύματος τὸ ῥαγδαῖον ἐγκαθεῖρξε. Ο. Immisch, however, who thinks that Cicero and Longinus are not referring to the same passage, would explain Longinus by identifying μικροὶ αὐλίσκοι with παρθένιοι (Athen. 176 E, 634 F), which owing to their extreme shrillness especially required the moderating influence of the φορβειά. Thus Cicero's poet means: ‘he blows no longer on a small flute (i.e. such as is not well adapted to a violent fortissimo, but requires the moderating influence of the mouthpiece), but a full deep note on a large flute without a mouthpiece.’ Sophocles, on the other hand, was referring to a musician who strained his delicate instrument by blowing too loud on it. See however Guhl and Koner, p. 209: it is not easy to understand why the φορβειά was any the less requisite on a more powerful instrument.

769

769 Clem. Alex. paedag. 3 p. 286 ἁβροδίαιτον ἐπονειδίζων νεανίαν ὁ Σοφοκλῆς λέγει ‘γυναικομίμοις . . . ἐσθήμασι.’

Bergk thinks that the reference to Sophocles was an error (Introduction, § 1), and that the passage actually intended was Eur. fr. 185, 3 γυναικομίμῳ διαπρέπεις μορφώματι, which has been recovered from Plato and Philostratus. The resemblance is close, but cf. Eur. Bacch. 978 ἐπὶ τὸν ἐν γυναικομίμῳ στολᾷ. Moreover, ἐμπρέπεις is shown to be Sophoclean by El. 1187 ὁρῶν σε πολλοῖς ἐμπρέπουσαν ἄλγεσιν, where the verb suggests by contrast the picture of Electra as a royal princess πολλαῖς χλιδαῖσιν ἐμπρέπουσαν (Kaibel). Nauck's critical note requires modification; for Stählin's edition, which has since appeared, gives ἐμπρέπεις without recording any variant.

lines.text: πρὸς δ᾿ οἷον ἥξεις δαίμον’ [ὡς Ἔρωτα] . . .
ὃς οὔτε τοὐπιεικὲς οὔτε τὴν χάριν
οἶδεν, μόνην δ’ ἔστερξε τὴν ἁπλῶς δίκην.

fragments.context:
770

770. 1 ὡς ἔρωτα delendum arbitror 3 οἶδε μόνην Plut., ᾔδει μόνον Clem. | δὲ στέρξαι Plut., δ’ ἔστεργε Clem.

770 Clem. Alex. strom. 2 p. 494 P. εὖ γοῦν ἡ τραγῳδία ἐπὶ τοῦ Ἅιδου γράφει ‘πρὸς δ’ οἷον . . . ἁπλῶς δίκην.’ καὶ γὰρ εἰ μηδέπω ποιεῖν τὰ προσταττόμενα ὑπὸ τοῦ νόμου οἷοί τέ ἐστε, ἀλλά τοι . .. τρέφειν τε καὶ αὔξειν τὸν ἔρωτα τῆς ἐλευθερίας δυνάμεθα. Plut. amat. 17. 761 F δηλοῖ τὰ περὶ Ἄλκηστιν καὶ Πρωτεσίλεων καὶ Εὐρυδίκην τὴν Ὀρφέως, ὅτι μόνῳ θεῶν ὁ Ἅιδης Ἔρωτι ποιεῖ τὸ προσταττόμενον· καίτοι πρός γε τοὺς ἄλλους, ὥς φησι Σοφοκλῆς, ἅπαντας ‘οὔτε . . . δίκην.’ vv. 2 and 3 are also quoted by Eustath. opusc. p. 305, 11 with the introductory words: εἰ καὶ μηδεμίαν χάριν οἶδε θάνατος κατὰ τὸν τραγῳδόν.

Η. renders: ‘And what a Power is he thou 'lt come before! That knows not favour, no, nor equity, But only cares for Justice absolute.’

The general sentiment recalls the famous fragment of Aeschylus (fr. 161): μόνος θεῶν γὰρ Θάνατος οὐ δώρων ἐρᾷ | οὐδ’ ἄν τι θύων οὐδ᾿ ἐπισπένδων ἄνοις, | οὐδ’ ἔστι βωμὸς οὐδὲ παιωνίζεται· | μόνου δὲ Πειθὼ δαιμόνων ἀποστατεῖ. Cf. Propert. 4. 11. 2 panditur ad nullas ianua nigra preces.

1 ὡς Ἔρωτα. ‘The context in Plutarch l.c. might at first sight suggest that Ἔρωτα was a vestige of words in which the poet described Hades as yielding to Love, though obdurate to the other gods (e.g. εἰς Ἔρωτα < μὲν | μόνον προσηνῆ, πρὸς δὲ τοὺς ἄλλους πικρόν, > ὃς κτέ.). [Mekler has since independently suggested almost exactly the same supplement: εἰς ἔρωτα < μὲν | πρᾷον πεφυκότ᾿, εἰς δὲ τοὺς ἄλλους βαρύν >.] But the context in Clement is not equally favourable to such a conjecture. Previous suggestions are : (1) ἐξερῶ τάχα Nauck. This (or ὡς ἐρῶ τάχα) might be supported by El. 35 ὧν πεύσει τάχα— followed immediately by the statement ἄσκευον κτέ. (2) ὡς στερρόν τινα R. Enger. (3) ὡς ἀγνώμονα Blaydes. (4) ὦ γέρον, τάχα Herwerden. (5) ὡς ἐρώμενον Welcker.’ (J.) R. Ellis preferred ὡς ἔρωτ᾿ ἄγειν, ‘for estimating love.’ It is curious that there should be a reference to Ἔρως in the immediate context of both authors who cite the fragment, since Sophocles appears only to have been concerned with the inexorability of Death. H. further notices that the phrase ποιεῖν τὸ προσταττόμενον (τὰ προσταττόμενα) is also to be found in both. Whatever may be the relation of Clement to Plutarch, if we suppose that their similarity is other than accidental, I should in any case hold that, so far as the text of Sophocles is concerned, the words ὡς Ἔρωτα have displaced the original script, and are to be attributed to a commentator who thought fit to compare the inflexible power of Love with that of Death, and had in view such passages as Ant. 781 ff., Trach. 441 ff., Soph. fr. 684. That such is the way of scholiasts hardly needs proof: a typical instance may be read in the scholia on Trach. 460. The conjectures mentioned above are based on the assumption that ὡς ἔρωτα is a mutilation of the original; but, if the view I have advocated is correct, it is idle to guess at the lost words. Tucker, following the same idea that occurred to J., proposed πρὸς δ’ οἶον εἴξει δαιμόνων Ἔρωτά τι. But, if Plutarch really intended to adduce the authority of Sophocles for the purpose supposed, is it likely that he would omit the verse which contained the pith of his statement?

2 f. τοὐπιεικές is contrasted with τὴν ἁπλῶς δίκην, much as we oppose ‘equity’ — in the non-technical sense—to the ‘rigour of the law.’ J. quotes Arist. eth. N. 5. 14. 1137b 11 τὸ ἐπιεικὲς δίκαιον μέν ἐστιν, οὐ κατὰ νόμον δέ, ἀλλ᾿ ἐπανόρθωμα νομίμου δικαίου. See also his n. on Ο. C. 1127. Cf. Eur. fr. 645: if the gods show mercy in certain cases, ἤτἄρα θνητῶν εἰσιν ἀσυνετώτεροι, | ἢ τἀπιεικῆ πρόσθεν ἡγοῦνται δίκης. Valckenaer (diatr. p. 188) gave a good illustration from Plutarch’s description of the younger Cato, who, following the Stoic pattern of the wise man (Chrysipp. II 640 Arn.), refused to deviate from the strictest norm of Justice: διαφόρως τοῦ καλοῦ τὸ περὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην ἀτενὲς καὶ ἄκαμπτον εἰς ἐπιείκειαν ἢ χάριν ὑπερηγαπηκώς (Plut. Cat. mi. 4).

lines.text: σκαιοῖς δὲ φαῦλον κἀν βραχεῖ διδάσκαλον.

fragments.context:
771

771. 2 ἐνικτῆρα . . . αἰεί L Clementis

771 Clem. Alex. strom. 5 p. 659 Σοφοκλῆς ὁ τῆς τραγῳδίας ποιητής φησί που ῾καὶ τὸν . . . διδάσκαλον,᾿ τὸ φαῦλον ἐπὶ τοῦ ἁπλοῦ τάσσων: vv. 2 and 3 are also quoted by Plut. de Pyth. or. 25 p. 406 F εὖ γὰρ εἰδέναι χρὴ τὸν θεόν, ὥς φησι Σοφοκλῆς, ῾σοφοῖς. . . διδάσκαλον.᾿

The fragment is variously interpreted. Brunck remarked: ῾ aeque vera videretur sententia, si duabus transpositis vocibus legeretur: σκαιοῖς μὲν αἰνικτῆρα . . . σοφοῖς δὲ φαῦλον κτἑ. Sed alterum tuetur auctoritas librorum. In his nihil decerni potest, quum ignoretur a qua persona et qua occasione sententia recitata fuerit.’ It is plain that he had no clear conception of the meaning. There is little profit to be had from the older versions, and C. W. King’s rendering of the third line — ‘ to fools a bad instructor even in trifles ’—is certainly wrong. J.'s note runs as follows: ῾ σοφοῖς . . . σκαιοῖς: cp. Eur. El. 972 ὅπου δ᾿ Ἀπόλλων σκαιὸς ᾖ, τίνες σοφοί; (“foolish ”—“wise”). By αἰνικτῆρα θεσφάτων it is implied that the god wishes to exercise the understanding of the “ wise, ” and to give them subtler or deeper lessons than suit the σκαιοί—not that he wishes to keep them in the dark. φαῦλον= ἁπλοῦν (according to Clement), “ simple ” : that is, he speaks in the language of φαῦλοι, the common sort, to those who can understand nothing more subtle: Eur. Hipp. 988 οἱ γὰρ ἐν σοφοῖς | φαῦλοι παρ᾿ ὄχλῳ μουσικώτεροι λέγειν. So Thuc. 3. 37. 3 οἱ φαυλότεροι . . . πρὸς τοὺς ξυνετωτέρους.᾿ J. evidently thought that the verses express the character or purpose of Apollo, that he chooses to be enigmatical to the wise, but straightforward to the foolish. I agree, however, with H. (Proc. Camb. Phil. Soc. 1907, p. 17) that both σοφοῖς and σκαιοῖς are to be taken as datives iudicantis—a view which seems to have been anticipated by Ellendt, who remarks: ’deum dicit sapientibus obscura et ambigua, stultis intellectu facilia portendere videri.’ H. points out that the interpretation adopted by J. cannot be reconciled with the meaning either of σκαιοῖς or of φαῦλον: thus φαῦλος does not mean ’simple’ in the sense of clear, lucid (τορός), or unconfused; and σκαιός, when used in a moral sense, always implies moral obliquity, i.e. it is equivalent to ’perverse’ or ’wrong-headed.’ He quotes Aesch. Prom. 637 λέξω τορῶς σοι . . . οὐκ ἐμπλέκων αἰνίγματ᾿, ἀλλ᾿ ἁπλῷ λόγω, Suppl. 473 αἰνιγματῶδες τοὔπος· ἀλλ᾿ ἁπλῶς φράσον, adding that the contrast is different here where φαῦλος and not ἁπλοῦς is used. H. renders accordingly: ῾ to the wise a hinter of deep meaning oracles, but in the eyes of the perversely stupid only a poor and meagre teacher.’ I doubt if this gives the tone of the last line. The wise view the god as αἰνικτήρ, and seek for an interpretation; the fool regards only the surface meaning. The attitude of the σκαιοί, who think that they understand the oracle but do not, is admirably illustrated in Dio Chrys. 10. 22-32. The clown (for σκαιός see on Eur. Hclid. 458, and Starkie on Vesp. 1183) thinks there is nothing to understand; Apollo is a plain person, of few words — like himself; an expounder in brief, μὴ ἐν πολλοῖς ὀλίγα λέγων ἀλλ’ ἐν ὀλίγοις πολλά, as Pythagoras recommended; no longwinded sophist, such as Protagoras, with his μακρολογία. (The difficulties of brevity the σκαιός does not realize: σοφοῦ πρὸς ἀνδρὸς ὅστις ἐν βραχεῖ | πολλοὺς καλῶς οἷός τε συντέμνειν λόγους Eur. fr. 28.) ἁπλοῦς ὁ μῦθος τῆς ἀληθείας ἔφυ (Eur. Phoen. 469) is the creed of the ordinary person (φαῦλος). Subtilty or elaboration, the refinements (ἀκριβεια) of the philosopher or the smoothness of the rhetorician, he treats with equal suspicion—ταῦτ᾿ αὔθ᾿ ἕκαστα, μῆτερ, οὐχὶ περιπλοκὰς | λόγων ἀθροίσας εἶπον, ἀλλὰ καὶ σοφοῖς | καὶ τοῖσι φαύλοις ἔνδικα (ib. 494 ff.). Just what Mark Antony feigned to be, ‘ a plain blunt man’ who ’speaks right on,’ that Heracles really was: Eur. fr. 473 φαῦλον ἄκομψον, τὰ μέγιστ’ ἀγαθόν, | πᾶσαν ἐν ἔργῳ περιτεμνόμενον | σοφίαν, λέσχης ἀτρίβωνα. φαῦλος was a word of censure, which those at whom it was aimed somewhat contemptuously accepted: so it is applied by Cleon in Thuc. l.c., by Eur. Bacch. 431, Ion 834, and elsewhere. Hence φαυλότης is the condition of the ordinary person, ’the man in the street, ’ who has no technical skill: Eur. fr. 635 οἱ τὰς τέχνας δ’ ἔχοντες ἀθλιώτεροι | τῆς φαυλότητος, fr. 641 ἐν τῷ γὰρ ὄλβῳ φαυλότης ἔνεστί τις, | πενία δὲ σοφίαν ἔλαχε διὰ τὸ συγγενές. See also Plat. legg. 966 E ὁ γὰρ ἰδὼν ταῦτα μὴ φαύλως μηδ᾿ ἰδιωτικῶς—he who has looked upon Nature scientifically never becomes ἄθεος. But the best illustration of all is in Plat. Phaed. 69 c κινδυνεύουσι καὶ οἱ τὰς τελετὰς ἡμῖν οὗτοι καταστήσαντες οὐ φαῦλοι εἶναι ἀλλὰ τῷ ὄντι πάλαι αἰνίττεσθαι ὅτι κτἑ., where Jowett's ‘ triflers ’ scarcely renders the point: the contrast is rather between the letter and the spirit (πολλοὶ μὲν ναρθηκοφόροι βάκχοι δέ τε παῦροι). Eur. fr. 162 κἂν φαῦλος ᾖ | τἄλλ’ εἰς ἔρωτα πᾶς ἀνὴρ σοφώτατος. It is not easy to say whether φαῦλον should stand alone, as I should on the whole prefer, or whether, like ἐν βραχεῖ, it is an attribute of διδάσκαλον. For the prepositional phrase qualifying the noun see El. 61, Eur. Hel. 1071 etc. — H. pointed out that τοιοῦτον in v. 1 may refer either to the following explanation, or to something that has gone before, as= ‘ of the like nature.’ Jebb on Ο. T. 435 supported the latter alternative. Blaydes’s conjecture ὄντ᾿ ἐπίσταμαι is mistaken: for the omission of the supplementary participle see on fr. 108. Naber’s κἂν βράχῃ—῾ even though he roar ’—is perhaps worth recording as a curiosity. — For the riddles of the Delphic oracle cf. Aesch. Ag. 1254 καὶ γὰρ τὰ πυθόκραντα (sc. are in Greek) δυσμαθῆ δ᾿ ὅμως. Eur. Suppl. 138 Φοίβου μ’ ὑπῆλθε δυστόπαστ᾿ αἰνίγματα. Heraclitus fr. 93 D. ὁ ἄναξ οὗ τὸ μαντεῖόν ἐστι τὸ ἐν Δελφοῖς οὔτε λέγει οὔτε κρύπτει ἀλλὰ σημαίνει. There is a similar — but political —contrast in Theogn. 681 f. ταῦτά μοι ᾐνίχθω κεκρυμμένα τοῖς ἀγαθοῖσι· | γινώσκοι δ᾿ ἄν τις καὶ κακός, ἂν σοφὸς ᾖ.

772

772 Demetr. Lacon in Herc. pap. 1012 col. 39 ὁ Σοφοκλῆς ἔγραψεν οὕτως· ῾ τόθ᾿ . . . σίκιννιν.᾿ Such is the restoration of Diels in Sitzungsb. d. Berl. Akad. 1897, 1073 of a very fragmentary original. His view has since been supported by Crönert, Kolotes u. Menedemos, p. 120 ff.

The words must have been taken from a satyr-play. For ῥυτόν, said to be a variety of κέρας, see Athen. 496 F — 497 E. σίκιννις (or σίκινις) was the satyrs’ dance: cf. Eur. Cycl. 37.

lines.text: Θήβας λέγεις μοι καὶ πύλας ἑπταστόμους,
οὗ δὴ μόνον τίκτουσιν αἱ θνηταὶ θεούς.

fragments.context:
773

773. 1 καὶ scripsi: τὰς codd.

773 Pseudo-Dicaearch. descript. Graec. fr. 59. 17 (Mueller, GGM 1 103, FHG II 259) αἱ δὲ γυναῖκες αὐτῶν τοῖς μεγέθεσι, πορείαις, ῥυθμοῖς εὐσχημονέσταταί τε καὶ εὐπρεπέσταται τῶν ἐν τῇ Ἑλλάδι γυναικῶν. μαρτυρεῖ Σοφοκλῆς ῾ Θήβας . . . θεούς.᾿ This is an extract from an extremely interesting description of Thebes included in one of three prose fragments of a treatise on Greek geography, which are contained in two Paris MSS of the 12th and 15th centuries (gr. suppl. no. 443 and gr. 571) and wrongly attributed to Dicaearchus. Mueller (FHG 11 232) was able to show from Apollonius the Paradoxographer (mir. hist. 19) that they were actually written by Heraclides ὁ κριτικός, who lived in the 3rd century B.C. (Schultz in Pauly-Wissowa Vlll 486). The extract relating to Thebes is translated and discussed by Frazer, Pausanias, v p. 27 f.

1 See cr. n. There is some error in the tradition, for which Salmasius conjectured τὰς πύλαις ἑπταστόμους, Brunck ταῖς πύλαις ἑπταστόμους, Nauck καὶ πόλισμ᾿ ἑπτάστομον (comparing Eur. Bacch. 919 δισσὰς δὲ Θήβας καὶ πόλισμ᾿ ἑπτάστομον), and Blaydes Θήβης . . . ἑπταστόμου. Headlam ejected πύλας, thinking that something had fallen out between μοι and τὰς: he quotes Anaxandr. fr. 41, 20 II 151 K. τοτὲ μὲν Σπάρτην τὴν εὐρύχορον, τοτὲ δ’ αὖ Θήβας τὰς ἑπταπύλους, and Tr. fr. adesp. 177 σὺ δ’ ἀμφὶ Θήβας στεῖχε τὰς Καδμηΐδας. The simplest remedy is merely to substitute καί for τάς; καί, as is well known, often disappears. The converse error occurs in Aesch. fr. 266. 3. Jebb on Ant. 118 understood ’seven-mouthed as to its gates,’ which is hardly satisfactory: cf. Eur. Suppl. 401.

2 ’The gods whom mortal women bore in Thebes are Dionysus, the son of Zeus by Semele, and Heracles, the son of Zeus by Alcmena.’ So H., who compares Pind. Nem. 10. 10 (of Argos) καὶ γυναιξὶ καλλικόμοισιν ἀριστεύει πάλαι· | Ζεὺς ἐπ᾿ Ἀλκμήναν Δανάαν τε μολὼν ἐτὸν κατέφανε λόγον. Weil (Journ. des Savants, 1904, p. 570), conjecturing θεάς for θεούς in the line as quoted by Dicaearchus, supposed that the text of Sophocles was modified by an admirer of Theban beauty. Stephanus corrected οἱ θνητοὶ θεάς, which he ascribed to Sophocles, and was followed by Bothe.

774

774. 1 καὶ ξυνίσταμαι P 2 πλεῖον vulgo edebatur

774 Dion. Hal. de comp. verb. 9 οἷά ἐστιν ἐν μὲν τοῖς μέτροις τὰ Σοφόκλεια ταυτί· ῾ μύω τε . . . φυλάσσομαι.᾿ Dionysius is discussing under what circumstances a reduction ought to be made in the contents of the κώλα, and suggests that this should be done when any of the words logically necessary are apt to offend the taste of the reader, and when their removal improves the style. He then quotes the present fragment as a case in point, since, if fully expressed, the second line would be ῾ πλέον φυλάσσων αὐτὸς ἑτέρους ἢ φυλασσόμενος ὑφ᾿ ἑτέρων.᾿

1 The words seem to describe the position of one who has been overcome by his enemies, and left by them as if he were senseless or in helpless captivity. Nevertheless he manages, without betraying his activity, to keep watch on their movements in the hope of foiling their plans. For the words μύω τε καὶ δέδορκα, ῾ with half-closed eyes I see,’ see Verrall on Eur. Med. 1183. They are less likely to refer to after-visions or dreams, as in Aristotle’s φαίνεται καὶ μύουσιν ὁράματα (de an. 3. 3. 428a 16). For the ironical antithesis cf. Eur. Alc. 521 ἔστιν τε κοὐκέτ᾿ ἔστιν (Hel. 138 n.). Hartung, who is hardly ever at a loss for a guess, refers the passage to the Inachus, supposing that it describes Argus being lulled to sleep by the incantations of Hermes. Rhys Roberts, comparing Hom. B 24 οὐ χρὴ παννύχιον εὕδειν βουληφόρον ἄνδρα, suggested that the idea might well be that of ’ uneasy lies the head that wears a crown.’ Herwerden conjectured κλύω for μύω.

2 φυλάσσων . . . φυλάσσομαι : the tables are turned, and the biter is bit. For similar collocations see on fr. 236.

H. renders: ’ I close my eyes and see and rise erect. Myself the watcher rather than the watched.’

775

775 Etym. Flor. in Miller, Mélanges de litt. gr. p. 32 ἄναξ . . . σημαίνει καὶ τὸν φύλακα, ὡς παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ, οἷον ῾ πύλης ἄναξ θυρωρέ.᾿

This metaphor is condemned by Arist. rhet. 3. 2. 1405a 32, quoting Eur. fr. 705, as ἀπρεπές, ὅτι μεῖζον τὸ ἀνάσσειν ἢ κατ᾿ ἀξίαν. No other example occurs in Sophocles, but Cope’s note requires to be supplemented by a reference to this passage. Similarly in Aeschylus κώπης ἄναξ (Pers. 381) stands alone; but in Euripides there are several instances, for which see n. on Hel. 1040. It is probable, however, that ἄναξ originally had a wider meaning than Aristotle contemplated: such at least seems the proper inference from ῾ Ιππῶναξ, χειρῶναξ, etc. See also Blomfield on Aesch. Prom. 45. Wecklein thought that ἄναξ could not have been addressed to an ordinary porter, and inferred that the words were spoken to Cerberus and taken from the Phaedra. The Heracles at Taenarum would be a more likely source (fr. 224); but the suggestion is too fanciful to be approved.

776 καλύπτει (καλύψει Plut.) πλευρὰ Plut., Suid., Greg. Cypr., Macar. | νῶτα : ὦτα schol. Il. | βοός : ἁλός schol. Theocr.

776 Etym. M. p. 26, 16 Ἄθως· ἀκρωτήριον Θρᾴκης. Σοφοκλῆς ‘Ἄθως... βοός.’ Schol. Theocr. 7. 76 Σοφοκλῆς ‘Ἄθως... ἁλός.’ The line is also quoted by several other authorities as proverbial (τὸ τεθρυλημένον ἰαμβεῖον Plut.) without the name of the author: Plut. fac. lun. 22 p. 935 F, schol. LV Hom. E 229, Eustath. Il. p. 980, 46, Suid. s.v. Ἄθως, Zonar. s.v. Ἄθως p. 58, Macar. 1. 46 (Paroem. II 139), Greg. Cypr. 1. 70 (ib. I 355), Cramer Anecd. Paris. IV p. 96, 18. As regards the reading, we are clearly entitled to prefer that of the authorities who expressly cite Sophocles: Plutarch, for example, who is nominally the earliest, is undoubtedly quoting from memory. The reading ἁλός (adopted by Campbell as well as by Pierson on Moeris p. 268) is given only by schol. Theocr. l.c., and is plainly an oversight, as J. remarks: shortly afterwards in the same scholia the v. is again quoted as Ἄθως καλύπτει πλευρὰ Λημνίας βοός.

βοός is explained as follows by the ancient authorities: (1) Macar. l.c. speaks of τὴν ἐν Λήμνῳ ἐκ μαρμάρου βοῦν, and similarly Suidas: τὴν βοῦν τὴν ἐν Λήμνῳ λευκοῦ λίθου πεποιημένην. (2) Plut. l.c.: ἐπιβάλλει γὰρ ἡ σκιὰ τοῦ ὄρους ὡς ἔοικε χαλκέῳ τινὶ βοιδίῳ, in agreement with Etym. M. (3) Eustath. l.c. merely mentions ἄγαλμα Λημνίας βοός. See further Crusius, Anal. crit. p. 69.

The distance of Athos from the nearest point of Lemnos is about 40 miles, and from Kastro about 44. [Eustath. l.c., who makes it 300 stadia, is approximately correct, and Steph. Byz. p. 36, 9 evidently followed the same tradition: it is absurdly exaggerated by Plut. l.c. as 700 stadia, and by Plin. n. h. 4. 73 (cf. Solin. 11. 33) as 87 miles.] The height of Athos is given in the Admiralty Chart as 6348 ft (1935 m.).

The shadow cast by Mt Athos upon Lemnos is also alluded to by (1) Apoll. Rhod. 1. 601 Ἄθω ἀνέτελλε κολώνη | Θρηικίη ἣ τόσσον ἀπόπροθι Λῆμνον ἐοῦσαν ... ἀκροτάτῃ κορυφῇ σκιάει, καὶ ἐσάχρι Μυρίνης, with schol. ib. ἡ δὲ σκιὰ αὐτοῦ ἀφικνεῖται, φησί, καὶ μέχρι Μυρρίνης (mod. Kastro, on west coast of Lemnos). (2) Plin. l.c.: Myrinam, in cuius forum solstitio Athos eiaculatur umbram. (3) Stat. Theb. 5. 49 ff. Aegeo premitur circumflua Nereo | Lemnos... ingenti tellurem proximus umbra | vestit Athos nemorumque obscurat imagine pontum.

The proverb is applied by Macarius ἐπὶ τῶν βλαπτόντων ἐκ γειτνιάσεως, and by Suidas ἐπὶ τῶν τινας λυπούντων ἢ βλαπτόντων. Somewhat more to the point is Eustathius: ἐπὶ τῶν ἐχόντων καὶ πόρρωθεν ἐφικνεῖσθαι ἢ καθικνεῖσθαι τῶν ταπεινοτέρων δι' ὑπεροχήν τινα. In Aesch. Ag. 296 the beacon-signal is passed from the Ἑρμαῖον λέπας in Lemnos to Mt Athos.

[The physical question raised by this interesting line, whether the shadow could in fact be seen, should be capable of determination by the observation of travellers. The ancient evidence quoted above, particularly that of Pliny, is fairly strong, and appears to be confirmed by that of modern times. Tozer (Islands of the Aegean, p. 248 f.), after speaking of the alleged phenomenon as an impossibility, remarks as follows: ‘At one period of the summer the sun is seen from this part of Lemnos to set behind Athos: of this I was assured by a resident in Kastro who had noticed it; and it may be inferred from Conze's remark that on July 2 he saw the sun go down a little to the right of that mountain. This also must be a striking sight, and one that would appeal to the imagination.’ Among Sir R. Jebb's papers were certain letters and memoranda which had been communicated to him by the Rev. J. B. Pearson, of Emmanuel College, Cambridge. Dr Pearson had made calculations which supported the occurrence of the phenomenon as being scientifically possible, and forwarded corroborative evidence from the writings of travellers. Thus Belon, Observations de plusieurs singularités (Paris, 1553), Bk I c. 25 p. 26v.: L'isle est estendue plus en longueur qu'en largeur, d'orient de occident, en sorte que quand le soleil va coucher, l'ombre de mont Athos qui est à plus de huict lieues de là vient respondre (sic) sur le port, et dessus le bout de l'isle qui est au costé senestre de Lemnos; chose que j'observay le deuxiesme jour de Juing (O.S., June 12 N.S.). Car le mont Athos est si hault qu'encores que le soleil ne fust bien bas, neantmoins l'ombre touchoit la senestre corne de l'isle.’ Conze, Reise auf den Inseln des Thrakischen Meeres, p. 109: ‘Ich sah am Strande von Kastro am 2 Juli 1858 die Sonne ein wenig rechts von Athos untergehen.’ Admiral Wharton, formerly Hydrographer General, wrote to Dr Pearson on 18 Oct. 1901 as follows: ‘Sophocles had every reason for his remark (Ἄθως σκιάζει etc.), supposing it to mean that the peak of Mt Athos would throw the ox or any point into shadow while the sunshine was still on the houses or hills near. It can scarcely mean that the shape of the peak would be discernible. It would be impossible for the apex, for the sun would be showing on either side; and the shadow of the edge would pass so rapidly that the eye would not detect it. The air is very clear in those parts, and I have seen the shadow of Mt Athos peak thrown on banks of clouds that must have been 100 miles from it. I was at Beshika Bay, twice the distance of Lemnos, and after watching the sun pass behind the peak, sharply defined against the bright sky, I turned round and saw this great “spectre of the Brocken” on the clouds.’ Dr Rouse tells me that Athos is a vast mass, very marked in form; and that at a distance of 100 miles he has seen it high above the sea. I am indebted to the late Mr J. Greaves, of Christ's College, for the following remarks: ‘I make the amount by which “dip” would lower the apparent height to be 1290 ft., so that the altitude above the horizon would be about 1° 13'. I worked out also the appearance of Snaefell as seen from the Cumberland coast. Its altitude would be only about 15'. The figure gives the appearance of the sun and Mt Athos as seen on the horizon from Kastro, and the sun and Snaefell as seen from the Cumberland coast.

When you take into account the extra clearness of the atmosphere at Lemnos, and the fact that Athos is isolated and Snaefell not, it is evident that the phenomenon of the sun setting behind Athos is a very much more remarkable one than when it sets behind Snaefell. I make out that the sun will set behind Athos about May 23 and July 22; but this is without taking refraction into account.... I do not know whether Kastro is at the sea level or not' [the citadel was in fact on a rocky promontory]: 'if it is above, the phenomenon will be more marked. The whole thing is absolutely clear to me, after consulting the map, working out the figures, and taking the clearness of the atmosphere into account. From Kastro Mt Athos will be a fairly prominent and isolated object on the NW. horizon, so much so, that I should expect the inhabitants of Kastro to say when May was advanced, “we shall soon have the sun setting behind Athos.” I should expect all the intelligent boys and girls to know the days when the phenomenon would occur. I am also quite sure that if the day was clear, the sun would be seen to set on July 2, 1858, a little to the right of Athos.

I arrived at Admiral Wharton's conclusions independently. If there is ground near higher than the “ox,” it would be in the sun-light, while the ox was in shadow, but I don't believe the outline of the shadow of the peak would be visible. The fact that the sun is a large disc and not a point of light would be against it.’]

777 Θεσσαλῆς Dindorf : Θεσσαλικῆς codd., Θεσσαλίδος Valckenaer

777 Etym. M. p. 123, 13 ἁπληγίς· τὸ ἁπλοῦν ἱμάτιον, ὅπερ Ὅμηρος ἁπλοΐδα καλεῖ. Σοφοκλῆς ‘τρύχει... ἁπληγίδος.’ Nauck adds Strab. 530 καὶ τὴν ἐσθῆτα δὲ τὴν Ἀρμενιακὴν Θετταλικήν φασιν, οἷον τοὺς βαθεῖς χιτῶνας οὓς καλοῦσιν Θετταλικοὺς ἐν ταῖς τραγῳδίαις καὶ ζωννύουσι περὶ τὰ στήθη, καὶ ἐφαπτίδας, ὡς καὶ τῶν τραγῳδῶν μιμησαμένων τοὺς Θετταλούς. I have slightly altered the ordinary punctuation of this passage for the sake of clearness, and believe that τάς should be added before ἐφαπτίδας. Even thus the sentence is awkwardly put together; for the meaning must be that the ἐφαπτίδες also were called Θετταλικαί. It will be observed that the quotation from Strabo is only relevant in so far as it attests that Thessalian ἐφαπτίδες (= χλαμύδες) were commonly worn by actors.

H. renders: ‘Wrapped in a worn shred | Of a Thessalian singlet.’

τρύχει. The word is almost entirely tragic, not appearing in prose before Aristotle. When used in comedy, it is paratragoedic (Starkie on Ar. Ach. 418). —Θεσσαλῆς ἁπληγίδος. The ἁπληγίς may be taken to be identical with the Homeric ἁπλοΐς, which was an outer garment worn over the χιτών, and thrown round the shoulders like a shawl or a plaid. It is contrasted with διπλῆ or δίπλαξ, which was a larger piece of stuff worn folded, so that it always required to be fastened at the shoulders by buckles. Both were of wool, and belonged as species to the genus χλαῖνα (Hom. Ω 230, ω 276). The Homeric ἁπλοΐς did not differ essentially from the later χλαμύς, except that the former was cut square, the latter round: see Studniczka, Beiträge zur Geschichte d. altgr. Tracht, p. 739, Amelung in Pauly-Wissowa III 2336. Thus it appears that Θεσσαλῆ ἁπληγίς is a description of the χλαμύς; for (1) we never read of a doubling of the χλαμύς in classical times, and (2) the χλαμύς was called Thessalian in virtue of its origin: Philostr. heroic. 3, 4 χλαμύδα ἐνῆπται, ξένε, τὸν Θετταλικὸν τρόπον, Poll. 7. 46 ἐντεθετταλίσμεθα ἔλεγον τὸ χλαμυδοφοροῦμεν, 10. 124. See Amelung, l.c. 2343. — Dindorf seems to be clearly right in proposing Θεσσαλῆς, which is the normal form in tragedy: the corruption was only what might have been expected, and would not have arisen so easily from Θεσσαλίδος (O. C. 314).

778 βλίττουσιν codd., βλίζουσιν Ellendt

778 Etym. Voss. p. 577 F Gaisf. (Etym. Flor. Mill. p. 66) βλιμάζειν... λαμβάνεται δὲ ἡ λέξις (sc. βλίττειν) καὶ ἐπὶ τοῦ τὰ κηρία τῶν μελισσῶν τρυγᾶν, ὡς Ἀριστοφάνης (Eq. 794) ‘ἀλλὰ καθείρξας αὐτὸν βλίττεις’ καὶ Σοφοκλῆς ‘ἢ σφηκιὰν... τινά.’

βλίσσειν comes from μ(ε)λιτιειν, strictly of squeezing honey from the comb, but metaphorically applied to a wasp's nest not as an equivalent for useless labour, but in reference to those who unnecessarily seek out trouble for themselves: ‘to bring a hornet's nest about one's ears.’ Cf. Ar. Lys. 475 ἣν μή τις ὥσπερ σφηκιὰν βλίττῃ με κἀρεθίζῃ. Macar. 7. 94 σφηκιὰν ἠρέθισας· ἐπὶ τῶν ἑαυτοῖς κακὰ κινούντων. Eustath. Il. p. 897, 56 (Ael. et Paus. fr. 160 Schw.) ἰστέον δὲ ὡς οὐ μόνον σφῆκες ὑπὲρ τέκνων ἀμυντικοί, διὸ καὶ παροιμία τὸ σφηκιὰν ἐκίνησας, ἤγουν βλάβην ἤγειρας κατὰ σεαυτοῦ. Ar. Vesp. 404 ἡνίκ᾽ ἄν τις ἡμῶν ὀργίσῃ τὴν σφηκιάν.

Ellendt preferred βλίζουσιν on the strength of Etym. M. p. 200, 34 ἀπὸ τοῦ μέλι μελίζω καὶ κατὰ συγκοπὴν καὶ τροπὴν βλίζω. But the evidence favours βλίττω (βλίσσω). For Schneidewin's view that the fr. is quoted from the Pandora see on fr. 484.

See cr. nn. ἔχω appears to be a certain emendation, but it is otherwise with Brunck's ἀγρίαν. Blaydes conjectured ἔχω δὲ χερσὶν νῦν βρίακχον ἀγρίαν; but the text may as well have been χερσὶν δ' ἔχω | ἄγραν βρίακχον.

Βρίακχος (or βρίαχος) is found as the name of a satyr on an amphora in the British Museum (790), on a lecythus in the Berlin Museum (2256), and on an oenochoe described by O. Jahn, Arch. Aufs. 14240. For the details see H. Heydemann, Satyr- und Bakchennamen, Halle 1880, p. 35 f. The text is the only evidence that the word was also applied to a maenad. Roscher in Curtius, Stud. I. 2. 122, followed Hesychius in interpreting it as crying aloud. He was no doubt right in comparing it with ἴακχος and βάκχος, but scarcely in deriving all three from ἰάχειν, ἰαχή. The first syllable of βρίακχος may have been identical with the βρι of βριαρός etc.

780 Etym. M. p. 265, 24 δημόκοινος· δημόσιος βασανιστής, ἢ ὁ δήμιος· ἤγουν ὁ ἐκ τοῦ δήμου τὸ φονεύειν κληρωθείς. Σοφοκλῆς· ‘οἷος... οἴχεται.’

The text has been suspected, not without reason; and the choice seems to lie between Bothe's ἡμῖν and Blaydes's δ' ἀφ' (perhaps better παρ') for γάρ. The sense appears to be ‘What a blood-stained torturer we have lost!’ For δημόκοινος cf. Hesych. I p. 482 δημόκοινος· δημόσιος βασανιστής, πόρνος, καὶ δήμιος. δημόκοινος was synonymous with δήμιος, ‘the public executioner,’ as is clear from Antiphon 1. 20 τῷ γὰρ δημοκοίνῳ τροχισθεῖσα παρεδόθη. Here it is almost certainly a term of abuse: Eustath. Od. p. 1833, 54 ἀπὸ τοῦ παρὰ τοῖς ὕστερον κολαστικοῦ δημίου, ἐξ οὗ σκῶμμα πονηροῖς ἐπέκειτο τὸ δημόκοινος ὃς καὶ ἄνδραχνος ἢ ἄνδραγχος ἐπεκαλεῖτο. So Lycophr. fr. 2 (Nauck, p. 817). Philo leg. ad Cai. 13 11 p. 559 M. ἀνδροφόνων καὶ δημοκοίνων θίασος. The executioner's calling made him necessarily impure. But from the interpretation βασανιστής a certain confusion has arisen, shown by the distinction which Herodian (ap. Lobeck's Phryn. 474) draws: δημόκοινος δὲ ὁ στρεβλῶν καὶ βασανίζων· δήμιος δὲ ὁ ἀπάγων τὴν ἐπὶ θανάτῳ. This distinction is held to be entirely unfounded (Thalheim in Pauly-Wissowa IV 2854), and is due to a mistaken inference from Isocr. 17. 15.

lines.text: τὸ δ᾽ ἔγχος ἐν ποσὶν κυλίνδεται

fragments.context:
781 Etym. Μ. p. 313, 3 ἔγχος...ὁ δὲ Σοφοκλῆς τὴν σφαῖραν ἔγχος κέκληκεν, οἷον ‘τὸ δ᾽ ἔγχος ἐν ποσὶ κυλίνδεται.'

The fragment is generally assigned to the Nausicaa, on the suggestion of Schneider and Bergk. The situation may be that of ζ 115, as described by Odysseus to Alcinous in η 290: 'the ball rolls close to my feet.'

Sophocles was a bold innovator in his use of ἔγχος, although it appears with the general sense of 'weapon' in other writers as well: see schol. Ai. 906 πᾶν δὲ ἀμυντήριον καὶ δόρυ καὶ ἔγχος καλοῦσιν οἱ νεώτεροι. So Pind. Pyth. 9. 26 λέοντι ὀβρίμῳ μούναν παλαίοισαν ἄτερ ἐγχέων. Hence the distinguishing epithets in Bacchyl. fr. 3 J. (13 B.), 8 ἔγχεά τε λογχωτά (secus Jebb), Eur. Her. 1098 πτερωτά τ᾽ ἔγχη (of arrows). In Trach. 1013 οὐ πῦρ, οὐκ ἔγχος τις ὀνήσιμον οὐκ ἐπιτρέψει; the sense is quite general, 'saving weapon,' but the intention is to suggest πῦρ καὶ σίδηρον, as in Anacreont. 24 τί οὖν; δίδωσι κάλλος | ἀντ' ἀσπίδων ἁπασᾶν, | ἀντ᾽ ἐγχέων ἁπάντων. | νικᾷ δὲ καὶ σίδηρον | καὶ πῦρ καλή τις οὖσα. But the most remarkable instance is O. T. 169 οὐδ᾽ ἔνι φροντίδος ἔγχος ᾧ τις ἀλέξεται. H. holds that this was copied by Opp. Hal. 3. 571 οὐδέ οἱ ὅπλον ἐνὶ φρεσίν, οἷον ἄρηρεν ἐκ γενύων. Blaydes suggested the insertion of ἡμῶν (or ἡμῖν) after ἔγχος.

ἱέμενον Sylburg ἱέμενος codd.

782 Etym. Μ. p. 315, 5 καὶ τὸ πῦρ (sc. ὁ Σοφοκλῆς ἔγχος κέκληκεν), οἷον ‘ἔγχος ἱέμενος,᾿ τὸ τὴν ὁρμὴν ἔχον.

I think that Sylburg was right in reading ἱέμενον (a change silently adopted by Brunck and Dindorf), as is indicated by the words τὸ τὴν ὁρμὴν ἔχον, i.e. set in motion: cf. Hesych. II p. 345 ἵεμαι·... ὁρμῶ. ἱεμένη περ· καίπερ...ὁρμωμένη, and ib. p. 346 ἵενται· ὁρμῶσιν, referring to Hom. χ 304. So Suid. s.v. ἵενται. lines.text: πολὺς δὲ πηλὸς ἐκ πίθων τυρβάζεται.

783 Etym. Μ. p. 490, 3 κάπηλος, ὁ μεταβολεὺς καὶ οἰνοπώλης. παρὰ τὸ χέειν τὸν πηλόν, ἤγουν τὸν οἶνον...τινὲς οἴονται ἓν ἀνθ᾽ ἑνὸς εἶναι, πηλὸν καὶ οἶνον, ἐκ τοῦ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ‘πολὺς...τυρβάζεται.᾿ ὁ μὲν οὖν Σοφοκλῆς εὐεπίφορος εἰς τὸν πηλόν. See also Cramer anecd. Oxon. II p. 455, 29; Etym. Gud. p. 298. 1, where the same extract occurs. It is mutilated in Suid. s.v. In schol. Ar. Plut. 426, 435 κάπηλος is derived from κακύνειν πηλόν, i.e. οἶνον. Hesych. III p. 31 πηλός· οἶνος. Ἴωνες. ἔνθεν καὶ κάπηλος ὁ τὸν οἶνον πωλῶν.

It is of course incredible that Sophocles used πηλός in the sense of οἶνος, as the grammarians admit (ὁ μέντοι οἶνος οὐκ ἔστι πηλός); rather it is the wine-lees stirred up from the bottom of the cask. Wine spilt on the floor was called πηλός: Plut. cohib. ir. 15 p. 463 A ‘πηλόν᾿ ὥς τις εἶπεν ‘οἴνου καὶ σπαράγματα στεφάνων.' Chariton 1. 3 οἴνου πηλὸν ἐποίησαν. Hence the joke of the μάγειρος, rebuking the clumsy cupbearer, who either spills the wine or lets the sediment mix with the liquid, μὴ δεῖν τὸν Οἰνέα Πηλέα ποιεῖν Athen. 383 C, Eustath. Od. p. 1401, 57. Demetrius de eloc. 171 ὡς καὶ τὸν οἶνον τὸν προχυθέντα ἐπισχών τις ‘Πηλέα ἀντὶ Οἰνέως.'

τυρβάζεται. Neil on Ar. Eq. 310 remarks that τυρβάζω is colloquial, if not coarse, and infers that this fr. as well as fr. 838 came from a satyric play. It is connected with πηλός also in Ar. Vesp. 257 τὸν πηλὸν ὥσπερ ἀτταγᾶς τυρβάσεις βαδίζων.

Suid. has a lemma κηρύκειος γραφή without any explanation. Presumably the words refer to the written instructions from which the herald makes his proclamation.

μόρῳ Α μύρῳ vulgo

785 Etym. Μ. p. 561, 28 λευγαλέον· τὸ ὑγρόν. παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ 'μόρῳ λευγαλέῳ' (so cod. A Etym. gen.: μύρῳ λευγαλέῳ codd. Etym. Μ. [μύρω λευγαλέ cod. M]). Cf. Phot. lex. p. 216, 16 λευγαλέα· διάβροχος. οὕτω Σοφοκλῆς: hence Nauck deduced μύρῳ λευγαλέα as the text of Sophocles.

This fragment has had a curious history. Sophocles, probably in one or other of the plays in which he reproduced the subject-matter of the Odyssey, imitated the Homeric line νῦν δέ με λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ εἵμαρτο ἁλῶναι (Φ 281, ε 312). This latter was explained by the comment τουτέστι, τῷ δι᾽ ὕδατος, which in course of time led to the erroneous conclusion that λευγαλέος and ὑγρός were identical in meaning: see schol. A Hom. Φ 281 λευγαλέῳ] ὅτι ἐκ τούτου οἱ νεώτεροι ἐξεδέξαντο λευγαλέον τὸν δίυγρον κτἑ., schol. Townl. ibid. λευγαλέῳ χαλεπῷ οὐ διύγρῳ ὡς Ἡσίοδος (does this refer to Op. 525?). τί γὰρ ἐπὶ τοῦ ῾λευγαλέοι τ᾽ ἐσόμεσθα (β 61)'; schol. Q ε 312 refers the interpretation τὸν ἐν ὑγρῷ (θάνατον) to οἱ γλωσσογράφοι. Nauck quotes Hesych. II p. 427 καταλευγαλέα· κάθυγρος, καταληλιμμένη, and schol. A Hom. Υ 109 ὅτι λευγαλέοις οὐ διύγροις, ὡς οἱ νεώτεροι. In the quotation from Sophocles the blunder μύρῳ perpetuated the delusion that he had employed λευγαλέος in the sense of moist, and the fragment was connected by Meineke (Callim. p. 245) and others with fr. 361. The truth was explained by Reitzenstein in a Rostock dissertation of 1891/92, p. 14, where he published the reading μόρῳ for the first time. Campbell, justly sceptical of the use of λευγαλέος, had proposed μυδαλέα. But the source of Photius' λευγαλέα (not λευγαλέῳ) still remains obscure.

lines.text: οὐπώποθ᾽ ἥβης ἐς τὸ σῶφρον ἵκετο,
ἀλλ᾽ ἐν νέοις ἀνθεῖ τε καὶ πάλιν φθίνει.

ἡβήσει τῷ σώφρονι ἵκετο codd.: corr. Pierson πάλιν φθίνει D (πάλιν φθείνει Μ): φθίνει πάλιν vulgo

1 f. The first clause has been variously interpreted, especially in regard to the meaning and construction of ἥβης. (1) Headlam in CR XVII 293 pointed out that σωφροσύνη is the proper virtue of old age (see however on fr. 210, 73), comparing Theogn. 1325 μερμήρας δ' ἀπόπαυε κακάς, δὸς δ' εὔφρονι θυμῷ | μέτρ᾽ ἥβης τελέσαντ᾽ ἔργματα σωφροσύνης. He held that ἥβης is temporal, ‘in the season of youth,’ and (apparently) by 'came to soberness' understood 'passed into soberness.' The objection to this view is that, if there is no reference here to later life, the balance of the contrasting clauses is destroyed. (2) Blaydes joins ὕβρις ἥβης 'the wantonness of youth,' and we might then take τὸ σώφρον as personal = τοὺς σώφρονας: cf. El. 1507 τὸ πανούργον. But the order of the words is decisive against connecting ἥβης with ὕβρις. (3) All difficulty disappears if we remember that ἥβη, like the Latin iuventus, is more flexible than our 'youth': the literal rendering is 'wantonness has never lasted till the sober stage of manhood.' Cf. Ο.Τ. 741 τίνα δ᾽ ἀκμὴν ἥβης ἔχων (of Laius). Trach. 547 ὁρῶ γὰρ ἥβην τὴν μὲν ἕρπουσαν πρόσω | τὴν δὲ φθίνουσαν, where Deianira is contrasting her own 'maturity' with that of Iole. Thus ἥβης is a partitive gen., for which cf. Thuc. 1. 118 ἐπὶ μέγα ἐχώρησαν δυνάμεως. Hdt. 8. 52 καίπερ ἐς τὸ ἔσχατον κακοῦ ἀπιγμένοι. Eur. Suppl. 709 ἀλλ' ᾤχετ᾽ ἐς τὸ κάμνον οἰκείου στρατοῦ. F. W. 3 Blaydes quotes Tr. fr. adesp. 574 ἅπαντα θάλλει καὶ πάλιν μαραίνεται, which he believes to be Sophoclean.

787

ὀργάσι Etym. Μ., ὀργάσασθαι Etym. Gud.

787 Etym. M. p. 629, 35 and Etym. Gud. p. 432, 53 ὀργάσαι τὸ πηλοποιῆσαί ἐστι καὶ ὑγρῷ ξηρὸν μίξαι. Σοφοκλῆς ῾θέλοιμι πηλὸν ὀργάσι (ὀργάσασθαι).' Hesych. ΙΙΙ p. 216 ὀργάσαι· ἑτοιμάσαι. καὶ ‘τὸν πηλὸν ὀργάσαι' φασίν, ὅ ἐστιν ἑτοιμάσαι, φυρᾶσαι, βρέξαι, ἀναδεῦσαι.

It has been conjectured with some probability that this fragment belongs to the Pandora: see on fr. 482.

788

φιταλιμῷ vel φυταλιμῷ codd.: corr. Sylburg

788 Etym. Μ. p. 803, 4 φυτάλιμος ... Σοφοκλῆς ῾προσῆλθε μητρὶ καὶ φιταλιμῷ (φυταλιμῷ VD) πατρί.’

φυταλμίῳ πατρί. The adjective signifies procreative ([Eur.] Rhes. 920 λέκτροις ἐπλάθην Στρυμόνος φυταλμίοις), and, when combined with πατήρ, the sire who begat (him). The force of the adjective is more or less accentuated according to the occasion: in Aesch. Ag. 339 φυταλμίων παῖδες γερόντων (or, with Weil and others, φυτάλμιοι παίδων γέροντες) it is merely pathetic. So τοῦ φυτουργοῦ πατρός in O.T. 1482, τοῦ φυτεύσαντος πατρός ib. 1514, τὸν φυτουργόν Eur. Tro. 481. τὸν φυτοσπόρον in Trach. 359 and φυτουργόν Eur. Ι.Α. 949 are more formal. In Aesch. Suppl. 600 πατὴρ φυτουργὸς αὐτόχειρ ἄναξ the lofty phrase expresses the pride of descent.

789

εὐνούχοις Bekk. anecd.

789 Etym. Sorb. ed. Gaisf. p. 1131 (Bekk. anecd. p. 1376) εὐνοῦχοι· οἱ τὴν εὐνὴν ἔχοντες, ὡς γεοῦχοι. εὐνούχους δὲ Σοφοκλῆς καὶ τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τοὺς εὔνεις καὶ ὕπνου μὴ μετέχοντας (μετασχόντας Bekk.), τουτέστι τηροῦντας 'οὐχ ὅπου...ὄμμασιν.”

For τηροῦντας Nauck formerly proposed πηροὺς ὄντας, but the text is better. The suggested derivation from εὔνεις (ὕπνου) is the grammarian's attempt to distinguish this application of the word from the ordinary meaning of εὐνοῦχος. But the bold metaphor (for which cf. fr. 761 n.) may be justified. In Erotic literature the λύχνος is the constant companion of the ἐρωμένη, either keeping vigil with her when she waits for her lover, or as the only witness of her meeting with him: see Headlam on Aesch. Ag. 881 τὰς ἀμφὶ σοὶ κλαίουσα λαμπτηρουχίας. Especially to the point here is Anth. Pal. 5. 165 ἢ νέος ἄλλος ἔρως, νέα παίγνια; μήποτε, λύχνε, | ταῦτ᾽ ἐσίδῃς, εἴης δ' ἧς παρέδωκα φύλαξ. The metre is doubtful, but the words are not necessarily corrupt.

790

790 Eustath. II. p. 1237, 22 διαγνωμονοῦντος Ἀχιλλέως ὅτι τε εὐψύχως ἔτι διάκειται καὶ διερῷ ποδί, καθ' Ὅμηρον (ι 43), ἢ χλωρὸν γόνυ κατὰ Θεόκριτον (14. 70) ἔχων, καὶ οὔπω δέος εἰς ἀλίβαντα καταπεσεῖν ζῶντι ποδὶ χρώμενον, ὥς φησι Σοφοκλῆς.

This extract, which is not quoted in sufficient fullness by Nauck, is a comment on Φ 301 ff. πολλὰ δὲ τεύχεα καλὰ δαϊκταμένων αἰζηῶν | πλῶον καὶ νέκυες. τοῦ δ' ὑψόσε γούνατ' ἐπήδα | πρὸς ῥόον ἀΐσσοντος. Nauck, regarding the sequence of the quotations, selected ζῶντι ποδὶ χρώμενον as the only part of the extract which belonged to Sophocles. But it is difficult to believe that the words οὔπω δέος εἰς ἀλίβαντα καταπεσεῖν were the composition of the grammarian who is the ultimate source of Eustathius. To disintegrate the actual language of Sophocles is another matter: we might write εἰς ἀλίβαντα καταπεσεῖν | οὔπω δέος νιν ζῶντι χρώμενον ποδί, or εἰς ἀλίβαντα καταπεσεῖν οὔπω δέος | ...ζ. χ. π., or as in the text. The first alternative gives an unusual tribrach in the fifth foot: see however Phil. 1302, Jebb on O. T. 719. The quantity of ἀλίβας is doubtful, though the a is generally stated to be long: see Adam on Plat. rep. 387 c, who however should not have spoken of the a as 'certainly long' in this passage. Schneider, Callim. II 254, argues that it was short, against Lobeck, Path. Prol. p. 289. Bergk wished to read χλωρῷ for ζῶντι from Hesych. IV p. 290 χλωροπέδῳ νεαρᾷ, just as Toup restored χλωρόν τε in Aesch. Ag. 682. But it is unlikely that χλωρῷ ποδί, if it had formed part of the original quotation, would have been corrupted in this context; nor is it by any means certain that the words ζῶντι ποδὶ χρώμενον belong to Sophocles at all. It should be observed that the purpose of the note was to bring out the contrast between the inert corpses and the vigorous vitality of Achilles, and that, though τε is misplaced, the clauses ὅτι τε εὐψύχως κτέ. and καὶ οὔπω δέος κτέ. are intended to balance each other. Cf. however O.T. 878 ἔνθ᾽ οὐ ποδὶ χρησίμῳ χρῆται, fr. 248. —εἰς ἀλίβαντα appears to be an equivalent of εἰς Ἅιδου. That Alibas was the name of a river in the underworld is stated by Suid. s.v. κήρ: λέγουσι δὲ καὶ Ἀλίβαντά τινα εἶναι ποταμόν (sc. ἐν Ἅιδου, as the context shows)· ἀπὸ τοῦ ἅπαντα καταξηραίνειν, καὶ μηδὲ λιβάδα ὑπάρχειν, ἤγουν ἰκμάδα: to the same effect Etym. M. p. 550, 33 s.v. κωκυτός. The river of Death parches instead of relieving thirst, like vinegar to which Callimachus (fr. 88) gave the name ἀλίβας. The ancients derived the word ἀλίβας, which has also the sense of νεκρός, from a- and λιβάς, i.e. deficient in moisture: see Plut. qu. conv. 8. 10. 3 p. 735 F, aq. an ign. util. 2 p. 956 A, Cornut. 35 p. 75, 9 ff., Didym. ap. schol. Ar. Ran. 186. The local habitation of the Alibas-myth may be taken to have been Metapontum in Lucania, which was at one time known as Alybas (Eustath. in Od. p. 1961, 62), and subsequently received its later name from Metabus, the son of Alibas (Etym. M. p. 579, 29). It is also significant that Metapontum was said to have been colonized by Neleids from Pylos (Bacchyl. 10. 120, Strab. 264); and that Pylos was reputed 'the gate of Hell,' and the original home of Hades-worship (Hom. E 395, Pausan. 6. 25. 2). Lastly, it should be mentioned that Alybas was the name of an evil spirit who infested the town of Temesa, on the borders of Lucania and Bruttium, until he was overthrown by the Locrian Euthymus: see the curious story related by Suid. s.v. Εὔθυμος. Cf. fr. 994 n.

791

791 κοκκοβόας vulg.: corr. Bothe

791 Eustath. Od. p. 1479, 44 (after speaking of κοκκύζειν as used of the crowing of the cock) ὑποβάλλει δὲ τοιοῦτον νοῦν καὶ Σοφοκλῆς, φασίν, ἐν τῷ ῾κοκκοβόας ὄρνις.᾿

κοκκυβόας is ῾chanticleer.᾿ Hesych. II p. 504 κοκκυβίας· ὄνομα κύριον, where Dindorf conjectured Κοκκυγίας (a wind), and Μ. Schmidt Κυκίβιος, both contrary to the order. H. thinks that the gloss may possibly be due to some misconception of Ar. Eccl. 31 ὡς ὁ κῆρυξ δεύτερον κεκόκκυκεν, where ὁ κῆρυξ is the cock. In reference to κοκκύζειν = ῾to crow,’ we have the dictum of Phrynichus (praep. soph. p. 35, 14 de B.) ᾀδειν ἀλεκτρυόνας ἀττικῶς· τὸ δὲ κοκκύζειν κωμικοὶ λέγουσιν. So Cratin. fr. 311 (1 103 K.) κοκκύζειν τὸν ἀλεκτρυόν᾿ οὐκ ἀνέχοντα, Plat. com. fr. 209 (1 659 K.) σὲ δὲ κοκκύζων ὄρθρι᾿ ἀλέκτωρ προκαλεῖται. Antiatt. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 101, 4 κοκκύζειν τοὺς ἀλεκτρυόνας· Δίφιλος Πλινθοφόρῳ (fr. 65, 11 562 K.). Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 47, 26. We should not infer that κοκκυβόας is below the dignity of tragedy, or on the same level as our ’cock-a-doodle-doo’: see Theocr. 7. 123 ὁ δ᾿ ὄρθριος ἄλλον ἀλέκτωρ | κοκκύζων νάρκαισιν ἀνιαραῖσι διδοίη, and Poll. 5. 89 καὶ ἀλεκτρυόνας ᾄδειν καὶ κόκκυγας κοκκύζειν—Ὑπερείδης (fr. 239 B.) δὲ καὶ Δημοσθένης ἐπ᾿ ἀλεκτρυόνων τὸ κοκκύζειν εἶπον. The latter statement appears to rest on the authority of Aristophanes of Byzantium (fr. 73 Nauck), from whom Phrynichus and the rest derive. See Miller, Mélanges, p. 428.

792

792 Eustath. Od. p. 1625, 44 λέγει δὲ καὶ (sc. Ἀριστοφάνης ὁ γραμματικός) ὅτι κατὰ τὴν δάμαλιν Σοφοκλῆς ἔφη ῾γηγενῆ βούβαλιν,᾿ καὶ Αἰσχύλος (fr. 330) ῾λεοντόχορτον βούβαλιν νεαίρετον.᾿

Aristophanes might be thought to have meant nothing more than that δάμαλις and βούβαλις are parallel formations, but in view of the fact that the extract is taken from his περὶ ὀνομασίας ἡλικιῶν, βούβαλις was clearly parallel to δάμαλις (νέα βοῦς) also in meaning. The Latin bubalus is said to mean both ‘buffalo’ and ‘antelope’; but Plin. n. h. 8. 38 condemns the former interpretation as due to ignorance: uros, quibus imperitum vulgus bubalorum nomen imponit, cum id gignat Africa vituli potius cervique quadam similitudine. Polybius was hardly open to Pliny's reproach, although some of his interpreters render βουβάλων as ῾buffaloes᾿ in 12. 3. 5. However this may be, the form βούβαλις is well established, and, so far as we can tell, denotes the antelope: with the fr. of Aeschylus should be compared Aelian nat. an. 3. 1, 5. 48. But it is not easy to understand γηγενῆ. Ellendt thinks it meant ‘wild’ (῾haud dubie ἀγρίαν, feram’); but I cannot find any authority for this, and should prefer ῾indigenous.’

793

793. 2 μητέρες αἶγές τ᾿ Dindorf: αἶγες μητέρες τ’ Eustath. 3 πόνον R. Ellis

793 Eustath. Od. p. 1625, 49 (quoting from Aristophanes Byz. περὶ ὀνομασίας ἡλικιῶν) ἔμβρυα δέ τινα καὶ ἀρτιγενῆ δὴ ψάκαλα λέγει καλεῖσθαι καὶ ὀρταλίχους. ὅθεν φησὶ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ῾ψακαλοῦχοι... ἀναφαίνοιεν.᾿ Cf. Eustath. Il. p. 777, 62 (schol. Hom. I 601 in Cramer anecd. Par. III p. 242, 33) ψάκαλα τὰ ἔμβρυα καὶ τὰ ἄρτι δὴ γεγονότα, ὅθεν καὶ ψακαλοῦχοι μητέρες παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ. Hesych. IV p. 305 ψακαλοῦχοι· ψακάδας ἔχουσαι. εἰσὶ δὲ ἔμβρυα.

The fragment appears to be a prayer for the increase of the flocks. Welcker conjectured that it belonged to the Ποιμένες, and Hartung referred it to the Inachus.

1 ψακαλοῦχοι. In addition to the above evidence that the young of animals were called ψάκαλα see Ael. nat. an. 7. 47 (who professedly follows Aristophanes of Byzantium) τὰ δὲ τῶν ὀρνίθων καὶ τὰ τῶν ὄφεων καὶ τὰ τῶν κροκοδείλων ἔνιοι καὶ ψακάλους καλοῦσιν, ὧν εἰσι καὶ Θετταλοί. The word is generally compared with δρόσος as used by Aesch. Ag. 147 δρόσοισι λεπτοῖς μαλερῶν λεόντων, and the Homeric ἕρσαι applied to very young lambs in ι 222. Giles (C. R. III 3), comparing ἕρσαι with the Lat. verres, suggested that the passages of Aesch. and Soph. were due to a mistaken imitation of the Homeric usage; but the evidence of Aelian indicates that ψάκαλον (or ψάκαλος) was something more than a literary curiosity.

3 γόνον should rather be γονήν according to the prevailing usage of Sophocles, although γόνον could of course be defended from other writers (see Lexx.). This consideration makes in favour of Robinson Ellis’s elegant emendation πόνον, which he supported by Aesch. Ag. 54 δεμνιοτήρη πόνον ὀρταλίχων ὀλέσαντες. The commentators on Aesch. are not agreed as to whether πόνον there is concrete (‘the young brood, their care’), or abstract (‘their loving care for their young’). If πόνον is right here, it would favour the former view, for which Eur. Phoen. 30 ἣ δὲ τὸν ἐμὸν ὠδίνων πόνον | μαστοῖς ὑφεῖτο may also be compared. — ὀρταλίχων, elsewhere only of the young of birds: Α. P. 5. 291 ὄρνιθες δροσερῶν μητέρες ὀρταλιχων. We may compare the transference of νεοσσός, and the more limited use of chick in English.

794

794 Eustath. Od. p. 1923, 61 λέγει δέ, φασί, καὶ Σοφοκλῆς πληθυντικῶς ῾σὺ ... βουλεύεις,᾿ ἤγουν παλαιά, ἀρχαῖα.

Eustathius is commenting on Hom. χ 184 σάκος γέρον, and quotes also γέρον γράμμα from Aesch. fr. 331. The adjectival use of γέρων, as applied to things, is found again in O.C. 1259 ὁ δυσφιλὴς | γέρων γέροντι συγκατῴκηκεν πίνος, where see Jebb’s note. Cf. also Aesch. Cho. 801 γέρων φόνος, and Soph. fr. 868. Nauck thinks the harshness of the present example would be softened by reading σὺ γὰρ <γέρων> γέροντα, Wagner preferred σὺ γάρ, | <νέος περ ὤν>, γ. β. <ὅμως>, and Naber proposed to complete the line with ἄγαν (lost before ἤγουν). Such guesses are harmless enough, but the proposal of R. Ellis βουλεύεις λόγον, after Eur. Her. 26, violates the tradition, which no doubt Eustathius faithfully preserved. The neuter plural perhaps occurs also in Etym. M. p. 227, 10 γέροντα πράγματα, but the reading is doubtful.

795

795 μολοσσῆσι Choerob. | ἐντείνων πέδας Nauck: ἐκτείνων πέλας Choerob., ἐκτείνων χεῖρας Anon. Ambr.

795 Georg. Choerob. exeg. in Hephaest. enchir. p. 60, 23 (p. 217, 15 Consbr.) τοὺς δὲ μηκίστους τὸ παλαιὸν μολοσσοὺς ἐκάλουν, ὡς Σοφοκλῆς ῾μολοσσῆσι...πέλας᾿ ἀντὶ τοῦ μεγάλαις. Anonymus Ambrosianus de re metr. in Studemund, anecd. I p. 227, 1 τὰ μέγαλα μολοσσικὰ ἐκάλουν· Σοφοκλῆς ῾μολοσσικαῖσι. . . χεῖρας.᾿

The text has been brilliantly and convincingly restored by Nauck, who points out that Μολοσσικαὶ χεῖρες must be understood not as ‘big hands’ but simply as ‘the hands of Molossians.’ In support of this use of the adjective he quotes (Lex. Vindob. p. 260) Eur. Hec. 1153 κερκίδ᾿ Ἠδωνῆς χερός. The Molossians would most naturally appear in a play connected with the fortunes of Neoptolemus, perhaps the Peleus or the Hermione.

lines.text: ὡς μήτε κρούσῃς μήθ᾽ ὑπὲρ χεῖλος βάλῃς

fragments.context:
796

796 χεῖλος Salmasius : χειρὸς vel χεῖρα codd.

796 Harpocr. p. 147, 17 παρακρούεται ἀντὶ τοῦ ἐξαπατᾷ...μετῆκται δὲ τοὔνομα ἀπὸ τοῦ τοὺς ἱστάντας τι ἢ μετροῦντας κρούειν τὰ μέτρα καὶ διασείειν ἕνεκα τοῦ πλεονεκτεῖν, καὶ ὡς Σοφοκλῆς που ‘ὡς... βάλῃς.' Dind.'s note suggests that Harpocration's Mss give ὑπό for ὑπέρ: 'vulgo ὑπὸ χεῖρα: sed codices tres ὑπὸ χειρός.' Bekker implies that all his Mss support ὑπέρ. Hesych. IV p. 332 ὡς μήτε κροῦσαι μήθ᾽ ὑπὲρ χεῖλος βαλεῖν· παροιμία ἐπὶ τοῦ συμμέτρου τασσομένη.

The general meaning of the proverb is indicated by Hesychius: 'Observe the proper measure.' Hemsterhuis well remarked: 'Mens Sophoclis est, sic animum institue ut in metiendo nec nimium vel parcus sis et alium defraudes, vel profusus et aequo largior, quod tibimet ipsi damnum ferat. Hoc dictum, quum venit in proverbii consuetudinem, monet medium inter opposita vitia utrimque reductum debere servari.' The details are less certain. κρούειν, ‘to knock, strike,' connotes a fraudulent act in connexion with measuring in the compounds κρουσιμετρεῖν and παρακρουσιχοίνικος (Poll. 4. 169). The former of these is interpreted 'to cheat in selling corn by knocking the measure and spilling the grain' (Neil on Ar. Eq. 859 κρουσιδημῶν). This appears to be the meaning indicated by Harpocration. It should however be mentioned that there was another method of cheating, in which εἰσκρούω (if not κρούω) was employed. This was to beat inwards the bottom of the measure, so that it held less: cf. Pherecr. fr. 105 (1 173 Κ.) λαβοῦσα μὲν τῆς χοίνικος τὸν πύνδακ᾽ εἰσέκρουσεν, Theophr. char. 30 (26 J.) Φειδωνίῳ μέτρῳ τὸν πύνδακα ἐγκεκρουμένῳ (surely we should read εἰσκεκρουμένῳ, with Edmonds and Diels) μετρεῖν αὐτὸς τοῖς ἔνδον, σφόδρα ἀποψῶν, τὰ ἐπιτήδεια, where J. renders 'with the bottom dinted inward.' As applied to weighing, it means 'to depress (the scale)': pseudo-Phocyl. 13 κρούειν σταθμὸν ἑτερόζυγον. Sophocles is not concerned with that, but it is possible that the variant ὑπὸ χεῖρα in Harpocration may be due to the influence of another quotation μὴ σταθμὸν κρούσῃς μηδ' ὑπὸ χεῖρα βάλῃς, in which depressing and lifting the scales were contrasted. Blaydes wished to read κρούσῃ, as if from κρούομαι used like παρακρούομαι.

μήθ᾽ ὑπὲρ χεῖλος βάλῃς, ‘don't overtop the rim,' is a clear case of tmesis in the stricter sense of the term; i.e., it cannot be explained except through the compound ὑπερβάλλειν. See on frs. 679, 799. For the general sense J. quotes Luc. ev. 6. 38 μέτρον καλὸν πεπιεσμένον σεσαλευμένον ὑπερεκχυννόμενον, where it should be observed that σαλεύω has an entirely different intention from that of διασείω in Harpocration. Neil on Ar. Eq. 814 points out that ὑπερχειλής means quite full, not running over, since χεῖλος is 'the lip in the proper sense, the saucer-like part above the neck of the vessel.' Cf. A.P. 12. 168 μεστὸν ὑπὲρ χείλους πίομαι. Η. adds Prov. app. 3. 89 (Paroem. I 433) μέχρι τῶν ἀμφωτίδων· ἐπὶ τῶν ἄγαν πεπληρωμένων, ἀντὶ τοῦ μέχρι τῶν ὤτων.

797

797 οὐ Bloch: ὁ cod.

797 Herodian π. μον. λέξ. p. 34, 3 ἢ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ‘ὁ σκέπαρνος...πληγαί.᾿ ὅτι γὰρ καὶ ὁ τραγικὸς λέγει σκέπαρνος ἐπ᾽ εὐθείας ἀρσενικῆς ἐν ἑτέροις ἐδήλωσα.

Herodian's position is that no genitive ending in -vos has p before it, with the exception of ἀρνός. Then he proceeds: αἴτιον δὲ τὸ πάθος, following as above. Lehrs altered ἤ to τό and added after the quotation οὐκ ἀντίκειται, thus making Bloch's οὐ not merely plausible but necessary. Egenolff however (Rh. Mus. LVI 291) inserts after πάθος Etym. M. p. 146, 19 ἔστι γὰρ ἀπὸ τοῦ ἀρήν ἀρῆνος, κατὰ συγκοπὴν ἀρνός, καὶ μετάγεται ἡ Blaydes compares El. 197 γενύων πλαγά. γενικὴ εἰς εὐθεῖαν, and continues ᾗ < καὶ τὸ > παρὰ Σ. Undoubtedly this is the explanation of πάθος, as Lehrs had pointed out. But I cannot follow Egenolff's further contention that his reconstruction forbids the change of ὁ to οὐ on the ground that the following remark ὅτι γὰρ κτέ. would in that case be meaningless. σκέπαρνος : σκέπαρνον is quoted as a new nominative parallel to the supposed development of ἀρνός. In itself οὐ is a great improvement, and recalls Ant. 249.

798

798 Herodian π. μον. λέξ. p. 42, 24 μάτη· ἔνθεν καὶ γενικὴ παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ· · οὔτι τοι μέτρον μάτας.'

Wolff for metrical reasons ingeniously proposed to insert the fragment before Soph. Ai. 870: but the meaning 'search,' which his suggestion requires, although supported by the schol. on Aesch. Suppl. 827, is rejected by recent critics of that passage (Headlam rendered 'clamorous lewdness'), and should not be assumed here.

For μέτρον cf. El. 236 καὶ τί μέτρον κακότητος ἔφυ;

lines.text: ἐγὼ δ᾽ ἐρῶ σοι δεινὸν οὐδέν, οὔθ᾽ ὅπως
οὔθ᾽ ὡς ὁ Τυδεὺς ἀνδρὸς αἷμα συγγενὲς
κτείνας ἐν Ἄργει ξεῖνος ὢν οἰκίζεται,
οὔθ᾽ ὡς πρὸ Θηβῶν ὠμοβρὼς ἐδαίσατο
τὸν Ἀστάκειον παῖδα διὰ κάρα τεμών.
